newsitem.title: USA: Republican in Louisiana runoff for U.S. Senate.
newsitem.headline: Republican in Louisiana runoff for U.S. Senate.

text.p: Republicans succeeded Saturday in pushing one of their conservatives into Louisiana's November runoff for the seat of retiring Democratic U.S. Sen. J. Bennett Johnston.

With 99 percent of precincts reporting in a state primary, state Representative Woody Jenkins, 49, an uncompromising anti-abortion leader and former libertarian, finished first with 26 percent of the vote (318,064 votes) after national and state Republican Party leaders unleashed a barrage of endorsements and ads on his behalf.

Former Democratic state Treasurer Mary Landrieu, 40, the only woman in the race and the consistent leader in polls throughout the campaign, came in second with 21 percent, or 260,325 votes, to edge out state Attorney General Richard Ieyoub.

Ieyoub, 52, finished out of the money in third place with 20 percent, or 245,879 votes, followed by former state Representative David Duke, a former Ku Klux Klan leader and Nazi sympathiser, who had 11 percent, or 139,580 votes.
Under the state's open primary system, all candidates run at the same time, regardless of party affiliation, with the top two vote-getters facing off in the November general election.
The campaign never captured voters' interest, and less than 50 percent of the state's 2.49 million registered voters turned out for the primary.

With Landrieu and Ieyoub running first and second in polls two weeks before the election, Republicans were faced with the specter of being shut out of the general election in Louisiana, one of four U.S. Senate seats in the South they hoped to capture. The others are in Arkansas, Alabama and Georgia.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee launched ads bashing Ieyoub for alleged questionable spending of campaign funds, while popular state Republicans, including U.S. House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston and former Louisiana Gov. David Treen, unveiled new Jenkins endorsements daily.
Going into the last 14 days of campaigning, Jenkins held a slight lead among six tightly bunched Republican candidates. By election day, polls showed him in a statistical dead heat with Ieyoub.
Political analyst Mike Baer said Jenkins' lead would have been greater except that Duke's strong showing in north Louisiana significantly reduced his vote.
Jenkins told cheering supporters he would vote to abolish the Internal Revenue Serice, repeal the income tax and impose term limits on federal judges, who now are appointed for life.
"We've had enough of federal judges that take prayers out of our schools ... and give abortion on demand. Only kings are appointed for life, and there's no room for kings in America," he said.
Landrieu, a pro-choice advocate, is the daughter of Moon Landrieu, a former mayor of New Orleans and President Jimmy Carter's secretary of housing and urban development.
"We can balance the budget, but not on the backs of our elderly, our disadvantaged or our families," she said. Landrieu is the first woman to make a U.S. Senate runoff in Louisiana history.

Since Louisiana initiated the open primary system 20 years ago, the runoff has always been between a Democrat and a Republican, usually very liberal versus very conservative, with moderate candidates cancelling one another out.

In the state's seven congressional districts, House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston, a Republican from Metairie, and Billy Tauzin, a Republican from Chackbay, were re-elected unopposed.

U.S. Reps. William Jefferson, a New Orleans Democrat; Richard Baker, a Baton Rouge Republican; and Jim McCrery, a Shreveport Republican, drew only token opposition and won easy re-election, with more than 70 percent of the votes cast in their districts.
